Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MOSCOW, Russia (CNN) -- Russian energy monopoly Gazprom said Thursday it has cut off supplies of natural gas to Ukraine after a payment deadline expired. A gas-compressor and gas-holder station in Mryn, Ukraine. Gazprom said it had cut supplies to Ukraine Thursday. Gazprom had been threatening the move, saying months of negotiations with Ukraine had failed to resolve the issue of outstanding payments. The company says Ukraine owes about $2 billion for past natural gas deliveries. Ukraine also disputes the new price set by Gazprom for 2009 deliveries, which was initially more than double the price from 2008. Gazprom has reassured the rest of Europe that its natural gas supply, which runs through Ukraine, will not be affected by the dispute with Kiev. Thursday, a Gazprom spokesman said on Russian state television the company had actually increased the deliveries to the rest of the continent. "Gazprom will continue supplying gas for its consumers in Europe at full volume," the company's chief executive, Alexey Miller, said. "We have an effective transit contract." Without natural gas, some Ukrainians could be in for chilly days and nights. The temperature at midday Thursday in Kiev was 25 degrees Fahrenheit (-4 degrees Celsius), with a forecast high of only 32 F (0 C) and snow predicted overnight.  Watch a report on Gazprom's threats to cut off gas supplies to Ukraine » . Ukraine's state-controlled energy company, Naftogaz Ukrainy, said Thursday it is ensuring domestic natural gas needs are covered by taking gas from underground storage facilities. "All of Ukraine's consumers are fully secured," the company said in a statement. In Washington, the White House urged a resolution Thursday. "The United States would like to see a restoration of normal deliveries," White House spokesman Gordon Johndroe said. "The parties should be resolving their differences through good-faith negotiations, without supply cutoffs." The frigid weather is of particular concern, the White House said. "We urge both sides to keep in mind the humanitarian implications of any interruption of gas supply in the winter," Johndroe said. Naftogaz Ukrainy also disputed Gazprom's claim that it owes for past deliveries, saying Thursday it has paid its debt to Gazprom in full, though it declined to give a figure. Another part of the dispute centers on Gazprom's price hike for 2009 gas deliveries. Gazprom had wanted to more than double Ukraine's payments, but Wednesday it offered a lower price. Ukraine, which currently pays about $100 per 1,000 cubic meters, balked at the figure offered, saying it simply can't afford to pay the new price. It is the second time in three years Gazprom has threatened to cut off gas supplies to Ukraine. The company made good on its threat on January 1, 2006, but turned the supply back on a day later. Russia is the world's biggest producer of natural gas and supplies Europe with more than 40 percent of its imports -- mainly via the pipelines through Ukraine. Naftogaz said in its statement Thursday that it would ensure the uninterrupted flow of Russian gas to Europe through Ukraine, but only under existing arrangements. It indicated some gas deliveries to Europe could be halted in Ukraine if Naftogaz fails to reach a new agreement with Gazprom. Although gas is still flowing to Europe, there are also concerns in Russia that the amount could be reduced if Ukraine siphons off some of the gas headed to the west. Naftogaz said it will continue negotiating with Gazprom to address the issues.

outputs.L2:
**MOSCOW, Russia (CNN) —** Gazprom, Russia’s state-controlled energy giant, announced Thursday that it had stopped delivering natural gas to Ukraine after the deadline for payment passed.

The company had warned for some time that it might take this step, arguing that months of talks with Ukrainian officials had not settled the dispute over unpaid bills. Gazprom claims Ukraine owes approximately $2 billion for gas supplied previously.

The two sides are also at odds over the price of gas for 2009. Gazprom’s initial proposed rate was more than twice what Ukraine paid in 2008, though the Russian company presented a reduced offer on Wednesday. Ukraine, which currently pays roughly $100 per 1,000 cubic meters, rejected the proposed price, saying it could not afford the increase.

Despite halting supplies to Ukraine, Gazprom has sought to assure other European countries that deliveries passing through Ukrainian pipelines will continue uninterrupted. A company spokesman told Russian state television Thursday that Gazprom had, in fact, increased the amount of gas being sent to the rest of Europe.

“Gazprom will continue supplying gas for its consumers in Europe at full volume,” Chief Executive Alexey Miller said, adding, “We have an effective transit contract.”

The shutdown could leave some Ukrainians facing cold conditions. At midday Thursday, the temperature in Kiev stood at 25 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 4 degrees Celsius. The expected high was only 32 F, or 0 C, with snow forecast overnight. A report examined Gazprom’s warnings that it would stop gas deliveries to Ukraine.

Ukraine’s state-run energy company, Naftogaz Ukrainy, said Thursday that it was meeting the country’s domestic demand by drawing natural gas from underground storage sites, including facilities such as the gas-compressor and gas-holder station in Mryn.

“All of Ukraine’s consumers are fully secured,” Naftogaz said in a statement.

The White House called Thursday for normal supplies to be restored and for the disagreement to be settled through negotiations.

“The United States would like to see a restoration of normal deliveries,” White House spokesman Gordon Johndroe said. “The parties should be resolving their differences through good-faith negotiations, without supply cutoffs.”

Washington also emphasized the risks posed by the severe winter weather.

“We urge both sides to keep in mind the humanitarian implications of any interruption of gas supply in the winter,” Johndroe said.

Naftogaz denied Gazprom’s assertion that Ukraine still owed money for earlier deliveries. The Ukrainian company said Thursday that it had paid its debt to Gazprom in full, although it did not disclose the amount.

This marks the second time in three years that Gazprom has threatened to halt gas shipments to Ukraine. On January 1, 2006, the company followed through on a similar warning, but restored the supply one day later.

Russia is the largest natural-gas producer in the world and provides more than 40 percent of Europe’s imported gas, with most of it transported through pipelines crossing Ukraine.

Naftogaz said it would maintain the uninterrupted transit of Russian gas through Ukrainian territory to Europe, but only under the terms of the current arrangements. The statement suggested that some Europe-bound shipments could be stopped within Ukraine if Naftogaz and Gazprom do not conclude a new agreement.

Although deliveries to Europe were still continuing, concern also emerged in Russia that volumes could decline if Ukraine diverted some of the gas intended for customers farther west.

Naftogaz said negotiations with Gazprom would continue in an effort to resolve the dispute.

Russia’s state-controlled energy company Gazprom halted natural gas supplies to Ukraine after the two sides failed to resolve a dispute over unpaid bills and the price of gas for 2009. Gazprom said Ukraine owed roughly $2 billion, including penalties, while the Ukrainian state energy company Naftogaz disputed parts of the claim and argued that Moscow’s proposed price increase was too steep.

The cutoff followed days of negotiations between Gazprom and Naftogaz. Russia wanted Ukraine to move closer to the higher prices paid by European customers, whereas Kyiv sought a more gradual increase from the preferential rate it had previously received. Talks ended without a new supply contract, prompting Gazprom to stop deliveries intended for Ukrainian consumption.

Ukraine said it would rely on gas stored in underground reserves to meet domestic demand. Officials maintained that the country had enough fuel to continue supplying households and key industries in the short term, although the dispute came at a particularly difficult time, with freezing winter weather increasing heating needs and daily gas consumption.

Much of the Russian gas sold to European countries travels through pipelines crossing Ukraine. Gazprom stressed that it would continue sending the full volume contracted by its European customers and said Ukraine was responsible for ensuring that transit shipments passed through its territory without interruption. Naftogaz likewise said it would honor its obligations as a transit country.

Nevertheless, the shutdown revived concerns that the bilateral dispute could disrupt supplies elsewhere in Europe. Previous disagreements between Moscow and Kyiv had led to reduced deliveries in several countries, highlighting Europe’s dependence on Russian gas and the vulnerability of major transit routes through Ukraine.

European and other international officials urged both companies and governments to return to negotiations quickly. They called for a transparent settlement of the debt and pricing issues and emphasized that commercial disagreements should not threaten heating supplies during the winter.

Although European deliveries initially continued at full volume, the cutoff left Ukraine increasingly dependent on its reserves and raised questions about how long it could withstand a prolonged interruption. The dispute also underscored the broader political tensions between Russia and Ukraine, as well as the strategic importance of energy supplies in their relationship.

counterfactuals.prompt: What happened when Russia’s Gazprom halted gas deliveries to Ukraine amid the 2009 pricing and debt dispute?
counterfactuals.output:
On 1 January 2009, Gazprom stopped selling gas to Ukraine after negotiations failed over unpaid debts and the price Ukraine would pay. Gas intended for European customers initially continued through Ukrainian pipelines, but Russia accused Ukraine of siphoning transit gas; Ukraine denied this and blamed Gazprom for reducing pressure.

By 7 January, Russian gas flows through Ukraine had stopped completely, disrupting supplies to about 18 European countries. Southeastern Europe was hit hardest: homes and public buildings lost heating during freezing weather, and some factories shut down or switched fuels.

After EU-brokered monitoring and negotiations, Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko agreed on new supply and transit contracts based largely on European pricing formulas. Flows resumed on 20 January. The crisis damaged both countries’ reputations as reliable energy partners and accelerated European efforts to diversify gas routes and suppliers.

counterfactuals.output:
## Gazprom’s $2 Billion Claim Rekindles Russia–Ukraine Gas Dispute and Raises European Supply Fears

**KYIV/MOSCOW/WASHINGTON —** A renewed dispute over Ukraine’s unpaid natural-gas bills has intensified tensions between Moscow and Kyiv, with Russia’s state-controlled energy company Gazprom claiming that Ukraine owes close to $2 billion and warning that continued nonpayment could threaten future deliveries.

Gazprom said Ukraine’s national energy company, Naftogaz, had fallen behind on payments for Russian gas. Chief executive Alexei Miller put the outstanding debt at roughly $1.9 billion, arguing that Ukraine had failed to meet its contractual obligations despite earlier assurances that it would reduce its arrears.

The claim came amid a broader political confrontation between Russia and Ukraine, adding an economic and energy dimension to a crisis already alarming Western governments. Gazprom has previously reduced or halted supplies during pricing and debt disputes with Kyiv, most notably in 2006 and 2009. Those interruptions also affected customers in the European Union because a significant share of Russian gas exports to Europe passes through Ukrainian pipelines.

### Gazprom warns over mounting arrears

Gazprom said the size of the debt showed that Ukraine was no longer complying with the terms under which it had received discounted Russian gas. Russian officials indicated that Moscow could withdraw preferential pricing and require Ukraine to pay a higher contractual rate.

Under a deal reached with the government of former Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych, Gazprom had lowered the price charged to Ukraine to about $268.50 per 1,000 cubic meters. The reduction was subject to periodic review and could be revoked if Kyiv failed to make timely payments.

Gazprom presented the debt as a commercial matter, saying it expected payment for gas already delivered. At the same time, Ukrainian and Western officials viewed the timing of the warning through the lens of the political crisis and Russia’s pressure on the new authorities in Kyiv.

A return to the higher price would place an additional burden on Ukraine’s already fragile finances. The country faced depleted state reserves, a weak currency and the prospect of painful economic reforms as it sought emergency assistance from the International Monetary Fund and Western partners.

### Naftogaz responds

Naftogaz acknowledged that payment problems existed but said it was working to settle its obligations. The Ukrainian company stressed that it had continued transferring money to Gazprom and argued that its ability to pay had been undermined by severe financial pressures in the domestic energy sector.

Ukraine sells gas to many households and public institutions at regulated prices below the cost of imports. Naftogaz has therefore depended heavily on government support and has accumulated large deficits. Poor payment collection and the country’s wider fiscal crisis have further weakened the company’s position.

Ukrainian officials also rejected suggestions that Kyiv intended to take Russian transit gas without authorization. They said Ukraine remained committed to transporting supplies to European customers and called for negotiations over the debt, future prices and the terms of continued deliveries.

Kyiv has long argued that its gas contract with Gazprom imposes an excessively high price and restrictive purchasing conditions. Russian officials, in turn, maintain that Ukraine must honor the agreements it signed and pay for fuel already consumed.

### Europe watches transit routes closely

The dispute immediately revived concerns in Europe, particularly in countries in Central and southeastern Europe that depend heavily on Russian gas transported through Ukraine.

Europe receives roughly a third of its natural gas from Russia, although the degree of dependence varies sharply by country. A substantial portion of those exports traditionally has crossed Ukrainian territory. Russia has reduced its reliance on that corridor through alternative routes such as the Nord Stream pipeline under the Baltic Sea, but Ukraine remains an important transit state.

European officials and energy companies monitored pipeline flows and storage levels while urging both sides to prevent a commercial dispute from disrupting deliveries to third countries. Seasonal conditions offered some protection: demand generally falls as winter ends, and many European states maintain gas reserves. Nevertheless, a prolonged cutoff could expose the most dependent countries to shortages and price increases.

The European Union has repeatedly called on Russia and Ukraine to separate transit obligations from bilateral disagreements. Previous disputes demonstrated that even when Moscow and Kyiv blamed each other, European customers could face reduced pipeline pressure within days.

### White House urges Russia not to use energy as leverage

The White House said the dispute should be resolved through normal commercial discussions and warned against using energy supplies as a political instrument.

U.S. officials emphasized that Russia had obligations as an energy supplier and that gas should not be used to pressure Ukraine during a period of political instability. Washington also called for the continued, uninterrupted flow of energy to European customers.

The administration said it was consulting with European allies about Ukraine’s immediate financing needs and longer-term energy security. Those discussions included possible financial support, measures to improve Ukraine’s energy efficiency, increased use of reverse-flow pipelines from Europe and efforts to diversify sources of supply.

The White House reaction reflected a broader Western concern that Moscow could combine military, political and economic pressure against Kyiv. Russian officials denied that Gazprom’s demand was politically motivated, insisting that any supplier would seek payment of a multibillion-dollar overdue bill.

### A recurring dispute with wider consequences

Gas relations between Russia and Ukraine have been contentious for years. Ukraine relies on Russian imports for a significant portion of its consumption, while Russia has historically relied on Ukraine’s pipeline network to reach European markets. That mutual dependence has repeatedly been complicated by arguments over prices, debts, transit fees and geopolitical alignment.

The latest confrontation leaves both sides with significant risks. A cutoff would worsen Ukraine’s economic crisis and could threaten heating and industrial demand. It could also damage Gazprom’s reputation as a dependable supplier and accelerate European efforts to reduce reliance on Russian energy.

For the moment, the immediate question is whether Naftogaz can obtain enough financing to reduce the debt and whether Gazprom will continue supplying gas while negotiations proceed. European governments, meanwhile, are preparing for the possibility that a bilateral payment dispute could again develop into a broader energy-security crisis.

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me the original report about Gazprom shutting off Ukraine’s gas in winter while promising uninterrupted deliveries to the rest of Europe.
counterfactuals.output:
The report you’re likely referring to is Reuters’ **November 25, 2015** article:

**“Russia cuts gas supplies to Ukraine, escalates dispute”**  
By **Vladimir Soldatkin and Natalia Zinets**, Reuters, Moscow/Kyiv.

It reported that Gazprom stopped supplying Ukraine after its prepaid gas ran out. Gazprom chief Alexei Miller said deliveries would remain suspended until Ukraine made another payment, while Russia maintained that gas transiting Ukraine for customers elsewhere in Europe would continue uninterrupted.

This is distinct from the larger **January 2009 Russia–Ukraine gas crisis**, when supplies to several European countries were actually disrupted. Because Reuters articles are often republished under altered headlines, searching the title, date, and bylines should locate an archived copy.
